title: WORLD OF DECISION
hook: On 14 October 1962, a U-2 flying over Cuba photographed Soviet missiles. Thirteen days later the world stands on the threshold of nuclear war. Take the seat of Kennedy, Khrushchev, Castro, Macmillan, U Thant, Pliyev or Arkhipov, and live those thirteen days again. Nukes, or chicken?
prologue: At 7:31 on the morning of Sunday, 14 October 1962, a U-2 of the US Air Force’s 4080th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing crossed into the sky over San Cristóbal in western Cuba at 72,500 feet. Six minutes later the plane was clear of the island, and that evening the film from its cameras went to Washington. No one yet knows what is on it.

Since the summer the Soviet Union had been sending 42,000 troops, missiles, tactical nuclear weapons and bombers to Cuba in an operation code-named Anadyr. In two statements, on 4 and 13 September, the United States warned against placing offensive weapons there, and Moscow replied that the weapons were purely defensive. The film will show whether that answer was true.

The story runs for fifteen days, from 14 to 28 October, and on to 20 November, the day the blockade is lifted. Of the seven seats, Pliyev’s and Arkhipov’s last only a day or a few days. Yet the nuclear button lay not in Moscow but right beside those two men.

A.title: Blockade and Bargain
A.text: At 5 p.m. Moscow time on 28 October, Radio Moscow read out a letter from Khrushchev: the missiles in Cuba would be dismantled and shipped back to the Soviet Union. The United States pledged not to invade Cuba, and the Jupiter missiles in Turkey were quietly withdrawn a few months later. On 20 November the blockade was lifted. The four submarines in the Caribbean were back in Sayda Bay by December; three of them had been found by US forces and forced to the surface.

B.title: The War in Cuba
B.text: The American air strikes began. The fighting stayed on the island of Cuba and was fought with conventional weapons only. The Soviet forces on the island did not use nuclear weapons, and neither did the United States. Even after the fighting ended, relations between Cuba and the United States never returned to what they had been.

after.text: The American plan began with air strikes by about 500 tactical fighters and carrier aircraft, followed by a landing led by two airborne divisions and a Marine division and building up to about five divisions. The U.S. medical plans, on the assumption that nuclear weapons would not be used, were drawn to accommodate up to 18,500 casualties in the first ten days. The chairman of the Joint Chiefs cautioned against taking that figure as an accurate prediction, and said that if nuclear weapons were used there was no basis for an estimate. The Soviet forces on the island, which the United States put at 8,000–10,000 on 22 October, in fact numbered close to 43,000, with 98 tactical nuclear warheads. On 27 October Moscow repeated its order that no nuclear weapon be used without its authorization.
after.src: FRUS XI d150, d186 note; JCSM-844-62 and CM-85-62 (NSA EBB 397 Docs 17, 22); intelligence report of 5 Feb 1963, Annex B; NSA [secondary]; order No. 76639

C.title: General Nuclear War
C.text: The strategic nuclear forces of the United States and the Soviet Union were launched. The war no longer stayed on the battlefields of Cuba or Europe, and the homelands of both countries became targets. No meeting was held that could have reversed that decision.

after.text: On 4 November the forces the U.S. Strategic Air Command could execute immediately were 1,479 strike aircraft, 182 missiles and 2,962 nuclear weapons. At first 66 nuclear-armed B-52 bombers a day flew airborne-alert sorties. A State Department analysis of 27 October put the Soviet Union’s operational ICBM launchers at about 75 and judged that the missiles in Cuba would increase the first Soviet missile salvo by more than 40 percent. In 1961 the Net Evaluation Subcommittee of the National Security Council estimated that, assuming a Soviet surprise attack at the end of 1963, 48 to 71 million Americans would be killed outright. Soviet forces in the autumn of 1962 were smaller than that assumption. In 1961 the Joint Chiefs assessed that a full American attack would inflict casualties on 37 to 54 percent of the Soviet population.
after.src: SAC historical study “Strategic Air Command Operations in the Cuban Crisis of 1962”; FRUS X–XII Supplement d434; NESC 1961 report (NSA EBB 480 Doc 7A); JCS reply of 26 June 1961

D.title: The Open Swap
D.text: The United States publicly accepts the trade proposed in Khrushchev’s second letter of 27 October: the Jupiter missiles in Turkey for the missiles in Cuba. The crisis ends quickly, but within NATO the trust of Turkey and West Germany is shaken, and Europe remembers that the United States bargained away its allies’ security.

E.title: The UN Freeze
E.text: As U Thant proposed, the blockade and the arms shipments are both suspended for two to three weeks while negotiations begin. Work on the missile sites goes on all the while, and the talks drag on.

F.title: The Missiles Stay
F.text: The United States keeps up the blockade but tolerates the missiles in Cuba. Forty-two medium-range missiles remain in the Caribbean, and in 1963 the next crisis comes in Berlin.

G.title: Tactical Nuclear War in Cuba
G.text: When US forces land, Soviet forces use tactical nuclear weapons. The nuclear weapons are used only in Cuba, and in the hours that follow both sides move to stop the war from escalating.

after.text: The Soviet forces in Cuba had 98 tactical nuclear warheads: 80 for FKR cruise missiles, 12 for Luna field rockets and 6 bombs for IL-28 bombers. On the night of 26–27 October one FKR unit moved to Filipinas, 15 miles from the Guantánamo naval base. On 22 October the United States evacuated 2,810 women and children from Guantánamo, and it sent 5,000 Marines to reinforce the base. On 2 November the chairman of the Joint Chiefs told the President that if the Cubans used nuclear weapons, the United States could respond at once in overwhelming nuclear force against military targets.
after.src: NSA EBB (tactical warheads, FKR) [secondary]; CM-85-62 (NSA EBB 397 Doc 22)

H.title: The Berlin Counterstroke
H.text: A Berlin blockade is added to the crisis over Cuba. It is the course Kennedy warned of again and again, at the evening meeting of 16 October and with the Joint Chiefs on 19 October.

after.text: The policy on military actions in a Berlin conflict that Kennedy sent Norstad in October 1961 (passed to the secretaries of state and defense as NSAM 109) set out four phases of response: small probes, economic embargo and maritime harassment, non-nuclear military action, and the use of nuclear weapons. Under the item on division-strength non-nuclear ground operations, the plan assessed that military overpowering of determined Soviet resistance was not feasible. On 19 October American intelligence judged that if the United States attacked Cuba the Soviets would almost certainly consider retaliation outside Cuba, and that Berlin was the most likely place. At the end of 1962 American intelligence put the Soviet forces in East Germany and Poland at 22 divisions and 1,200 tactical aircraft. West Berlin’s stocks, with selective rationing, were food for six months or more and coal for about a year.
after.src: FRUS XIV d185; FRUS XI d32 (SNIE 11-18-62); FRUS VIII d117 (NIE 11-1-62); FRUS XV d139

I.title: Limited Nuclear War in Europe
I.text: Nuclear weapons were used on battlefields outside Cuba. They were used in Turkey or in Europe, but the United States and the Soviet Union did not attack each other’s homeland, and a cease-fire took effect under UN supervision. The war stopped at the step the 1961 American Berlin contingency plan had placed just before general nuclear war.

after.text: The last phase of the Berlin contingency plan listed three courses: selective nuclear attacks to demonstrate the will to use nuclear weapons, limited nuclear use for tactical advantage, and general nuclear war. The plan warned that if the allies took limited nuclear action first, it might bring a reply in kind, and might also prompt an unrestrained pre-emptive attack. There were 15 Jupiter missiles near İzmir in Turkey and 30 in Italy. On 22 October the President ordered that the Jupiters not be fired even if attacked. On 27 October Secretary of Defense McNamara said that if the Soviets attacked Turkey the United States must respond in the NATO area, and that the minimum response would be an attack on the Black Sea Fleet. At a NATO meeting in 1963 he said that the number of tactical nuclear weapons in Europe had increased by almost 60 percent since early 1961.
after.src: FRUS XIV d185; FRUS XI d40, d94; NSA EBB 821 [secondary]; NATO RDC-63-497

J.title: Nuclear War at Sea
J.text: In the quarantine waters of the Atlantic northeast of Cuba, a Soviet submarine’s nuclear torpedo exploded. An American destroyer sank, and the submarine did not come home either. Both sides stopped at sea, and no nuclear weapon was used on land. The missile crisis then continued through letters and the mediation of the United Nations.

after.text: The four Soviet submarines bound for Cuba (B-4, B-36, B-59, B-130) each carried one nuclear torpedo. Their captains recalled oral instructions to use them if attacked by the Americans and hulled; no written order has been found. The U.S. Navy drew its quarantine line on an arc 500 miles from Cape Maisí, and the ASW carriers Essex and Randolph hunted the submarines with their destroyers. On 27 October B-59 surfaced amid the signaling depth charges of an American anti-submarine group. No document of the time has been found on the yield of the nuclear torpedo or on damage to ships.
after.src: NSA EBB 75, 399, 808; Navy Department Library, The Naval Quarantine of Cuba

history: By 2 November all the missiles had been made inoperable, and on 4 November Kuznetsov stated that as of 22 October 24 launch sites had been complete and 16 unfinished, and that there were 42 missiles. The 42 sailed on nine ships by 8 November, and the US Navy checked the missiles on deck at sea, by eye and by photograph. The withdrawal of the Il-28 bombers was agreed on 19–20 November and carried out in December. Kennedy’s press conference on 20 November lifted the blockade, and SAC’s airborne alert ended the same day. The 98 tactical nuclear warheads still in Cuba were ordered out that day and left aboard the Atkarsk on 1 December.

A rift remained between Cuba and the Soviet Union. Mikoyan stayed in Havana from 2 to 26 November to bring Castro round, and at the Presidium on 3 December Malinovsky and Kosygin called the Cubans “unreliable allies.” At the same meeting Khrushchev summed up the outcome as a victory, saying that “anyone who says we retreated is being malicious.” But in a long letter to Castro on 31 January 1963 he admitted that a rift remained between the two countries and invited him to visit the Soviet Union. Castro went that spring.

The last Jupiter in Turkey came down on 24 April 1963, and Polaris submarines took their place. Within the alliance, other verdicts lingered. Under Secretary of State Ball reported on 19 November that when he briefed the NATO Council in Paris, the reaction had been uniform: the United States had let the Russians off too easily. Strong, the head of British intelligence, reported that the United States had been ready to act alone without consulting its allies, and Macmillan and Home put American “overconfidence” on the agenda for the next summit.

On 20 June 1963 in Geneva, the United States and the Soviet Union agreed to set up a direct communications link between Washington and Moscow, the hotline, and on 5 August in Moscow the United States, Britain and the Soviet Union signed the Partial Test Ban Treaty, which banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, under water and in outer space. Khrushchev was removed by the Party Central Committee on 14 October 1964, and the colleagues who ousted him counted the Cuban adventure among his blunders.

The full story came out over decades. In 1990 the Cuban government released the letters exchanged between Castro and Khrushchev. At the Havana conference of January 1992, Castro attended in person and spoke at length, and General Gribkov startled the American participants by revealing that there had been tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba. The 40th-anniversary conference in Havana in 2002 and Soviet naval documents released the same year brought out the story of B-59 and its nuclear torpedo, and a full English translation of the Malin notes, the record of the Presidium’s meetings, appeared in a Wilson Center bulletin in 2012. Recordings of the White House meetings have been released in stages since the 1980s, and the transcripts exist in several editions.
eastasia: After the crisis, China openly criticized the Soviet Union: sending the missiles had been “adventurism,” and withdrawing them under American pressure “capitulationism.” The Soviets retorted that China did not understand the danger of nuclear war, and in the summer of 1963 the two communist parties denounced each other in open letters and split. The Cuban crisis was one of the moments at which the Sino-Soviet dispute passed beyond hiding.

At the same time, China and India were at war in the Himalayas. Chinese forces attacked in Ladakh and on the northeastern frontier on 20 October and declared a unilateral ceasefire on 21 November, a span that almost coincides with the thirteen days of the Cuban crisis. The Soviet Presidium’s minutes for 11 and 14 October carry no item on Cuba, only the India–China dispute. During the crisis the Soviet Union leaned toward China; once it was over, Moscow turned back toward India.

US forces in Korea and Japan went on alert as well. With Kennedy’s speech on 22 October, DEFCON 3 was ordered for all US forces worldwide, and SAC went to DEFCON 2 on 24 October. The garrisons in South Korea, Japan and Okinawa were under this alert too. SAC came down from DEFCON 2 on 15 November, and the remaining alerts were lowered on 20 November, the day the blockade was lifted.

background.q: Why did Khrushchev send the missiles?
a: The decision was made in May 1962. At the Presidium on 21 May, Khrushchev said he would conclude a joint defense treaty with Castro and deploy nuclear missiles, in secret, announcing them only afterward, and that the missiles would stay under Soviet command; he himself called it an “offensive policy.” The Presidium approved the plan on 24 May, and a memorandum from Defense Minister Malinovsky that day listed 24 R-12 (SS-4) launchers and 16 R-14 (SS-5) launchers, 60 missiles and 60 warheads, about 44,000 troops and 70–80 ships. The code name was “Anadyr.”

Khrushchev himself gave two reasons. In June, in the Kremlin, he told the generals leaving for Cuba that the point was to “throw a hedgehog” at the Americans so that they could not swallow Cuba; in his memoirs he wrote that the idea came to him on a visit to Bulgaria in May, as he thought about the American missiles in Turkey. At the Presidium on the night of 22 October he said, “We did not want to unleash a war; we wanted to intimidate them, to deter the USA.”

Historians are divided. Some think the defense of Cuba was the main aim; some that Khrushchev meant to overturn at a stroke a nuclear balance in which the United States was far ahead; others that he wanted a bargaining chip to trade over Berlin and the overseas bases. At the time, British intelligence judged in a briefing on 23 October that Moscow meant to present the deployment as a fait accompli in November and then bargain over Berlin and the bases.

In the end, secrecy worked against the Soviet Union. In the summer Castro asked for the treaty to be signed in public, but Khrushchev insisted on secrecy, and a TASS statement on 11 September declared that the arms sent to Cuba were purely defensive. In his report after the crisis, Marshal Biryuzov wrote that the main reason for the discovery was the failure to conceal the launch areas properly, and at the 1992 conference Castro recalled that the secrecy had put Cuba at a political disadvantage.

background.q: Why did Kennedy choose a blockade over an air strike?
a: At the first meeting on 16 October, Kennedy said that one way or another “we’re going to take out these missiles.” General Taylor, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, wanted to strike without any warning, and Vice President Johnson also favored an air strike. The options raised that day were a strike on the missile sites alone, a full air strike that would also hit airfields and air defenses, an air strike combined with a blockade, an invasion, and a political track of advance warning and negotiation.

Over three days the weaknesses of an air strike came out. On 21 October the Air Force reported that it could destroy no more than 90 percent of the known missiles, and those at the meetings agreed that an air strike would lead in the end to an invasion. Defense Secretary McNamara thought that if several hundred Soviet troops were killed, the price would be paid in Berlin, and Robert Kennedy said again and again that a surprise attack would recall Pearl Harbor. On 19 October, when the Air Force chief of staff, LeMay, called the blockade “almost as bad as the appeasement at Munich,” the President answered, in effect, that LeMay was in the same boat.

The blockade was decided at the National Security Council on 20 October, and at the suggestion of Secretary of State Rusk it was named a “quarantine.” Ormsby-Gore, the British ambassador, who was first told over lunch the next day, also backed the blockade, arguing that an air strike would cost the United States politically. On 22 October the congressional leaders called for an immediate air strike, as Senator Russell did when he asked “why wait?”, but Kennedy explained that killing Soviet troops would be far more provocative than a confrontation between ships.

The blockade was a first step, not the end. The air strike plans stayed ready for execution all that week, and on 27 October the Joint Chiefs recommended an air strike on Monday and an invasion seven days later. On 26 October Kennedy himself said the missiles could be got out “only by invasion or by a trade.” Some read the blockade as buying the time that made a deal possible; others point out that the blockade by itself did not remove a single missile.

background.q: How was the deal over the Jupiters in Turkey struck?
a: Turkey had 15 American Jupiter intermediate-range missiles. Kennedy had wanted them out even before the crisis, and in a directive of 23 August he asked, “What action can be taken to get Jupiter missiles out of Turkey?” At the meeting on the morning of 27 October he said he had wanted them withdrawn for more than a year because they were obsolete, and that if the United States appeared to attack Cuba to protect useless missiles, it would be in a bad position.

That same day Moscow broadcast a second letter on the radio which, unlike the letter of the day before, made the withdrawal of the missiles in Turkey a condition. At the Presidium Khrushchev said that if they got the bases in Turkey removed as well, they would have won. In Washington, Nitze said it would be “anathema to the Turks,” Bundy said the United States could not be seen selling out an ally, and General Norstad, the NATO commander, also advised rejection. Macmillan added his weight to rejection too, arguing that no one could escape his own danger with a deal that sacrificed an ally.

The way out was a private understanding. At 7:45 p.m. on 27 October Robert Kennedy met Ambassador Dobrynin and handed him the public letter answering the letter of 26 October, and told him orally that the missiles in Turkey were not part of any deal but would be gone within a few months of the crisis ending. In his own memorandum the sentence about “four to five months” was crossed out; in Dobrynin’s cable the words remained. On 28 October Moscow decided to keep this part strictly secret, and Khrushchev’s letter confirming it, which Dobrynin delivered on 29 October, Robert Kennedy handed back the next day.

The promise was kept. At the NATO ministerial meeting in Paris in December, McNamara proposed dismantling the Jupiters in Turkey and Italy and replacing them with Polaris submarines; the Turkish cabinet agreed on 9 February 1963, and the last Jupiter in Turkey came down on 24 April 1963. Opinions differ on whether this was a deal. Rusk wrote in 1987 that it was no deal, since the Jupiters were coming out anyway; some historians see the private condition as the key that changed the outcome.

Castro learned of Khrushchev’s decision to withdraw from a Radio Moscow broadcast on the morning of 28 October, and received the letter addressed to him only an hour or two later. He later recalled feeling “not relief but deep indignation.” That same day the Cuban government declared five conditions: an end to the economic blockade, an end to subversive activities, an end to pirate attacks, an end to violations of Cuban airspace and territorial waters, and withdrawal from Guantánamo.

The refusal of inspection did not begin that day. In his national address on the night of 23 October he had already rejected UN observers, and in his reply to Khrushchev on the evening of 28 October he wrote that he opposed inspection on principle. To U Thant, who came to Havana on 30 October, he said that inspection could be imposed only on a conquered country, that Cuba was not Austria, nor the Sudetenland, nor the Congo, and he also rejected a plan to inspect ships in port. On 5 November he told Mikoyan that one-sided inspection would do terrible harm to the people’s morale.

Behind it lay distrust of the Soviet Union. Castro had wanted the treaty made public since the summer but had been held to secrecy; he was hurt that Khrushchev read the letter he wrote on the night of 26 October as a proposal for a nuclear first strike; and after receiving Khrushchev’s long letter of 30 October he said, “It is not some comrades but the whole people who do not understand.” In November he refused to see Mikoyan for three days in protest at the withdrawal of the Il-28 bombers.

In the end there was no inspection on the ground. From early November the United States made do by checking the missiles by eye and by photograph from alongside the departing Soviet ships, and when it lifted the blockade on 20 November it gave its pledge not to invade only informally, not in an official document. Some see Castro’s refusal as a matter of sovereignty and prestige; others as an expression of his distrust of the Soviet Union.

background.q: Why was there a nuclear torpedo aboard B-59?
a: The four Foxtrot-class submarines of the Northern Fleet’s 69th Brigade each carried 22 torpedoes, one of them nuclear. A navy report of 25 September 1962 set out the plan: each submarine of the brigade would carry one nuclear torpedo, and the brigade would escort the Aleksandrovsk, which carried warheads. Since it had been decided not to send a squadron of surface ships, cruisers included, these four submarines were very nearly the whole of the Soviet naval force sent to Cuban waters.

The four left Sayda Bay between 30 September and the small hours of 1 October. A few hours before sailing, the commanders received “top secret” envelopes to be opened after passing Kola Bay. Paragraph 8 of the combat instructions said that weapons were to be kept at combat readiness during the voyage but that conventional torpedoes were to be used only on the orders of the commander-in-chief of the navy or if the submarine came under attack. The conditions for firing the nuclear torpedo were passed on not in writing but only orally, by Admiral Fokin and Rassokho, the chief of staff, and accounts of what they said differ.

On the afternoon of 27 October B-59 was surrounded by the carrier USS Randolph and nine destroyers and subjected to practice depth charges for about four hours. The batteries were nearly exhausted and only the emergency lights were on; the temperature inside rose to 45–60°C, and carbon dioxide reached its limit, so that men on watch collapsed one after another. According to Orlov’s recollections, Captain Savitsky ordered the nuclear torpedo readied, saying war might already have begun up above, but after consulting Arkhipov, the brigade chief of staff, and Maslennikov, the political officer, he decided to surface. Once B-59 was on the surface, US aircraft made 12 low passes and fired about 300 cannon rounds, and in a 1997 presentation Arkhipov wrote that a crash dive at that moment “would have meant war.”

In 1962 the United States did not know these submarines carried nuclear torpedoes. That became widely known only through the Havana conference marking the crisis’s 40th anniversary in 2002, Soviet documents released the same year, and Orlov’s recollections. The usual view is that the Soviets sent the nuclear torpedoes to take on American carrier groups if war came. Yet although Khrushchev told an American businessman on 24 October that the missiles would be fired only on his personal order, the nuclear weapons aboard the submarines were almost beyond Moscow’s reach.

It is widely said that the nuclear torpedo could be fired only if three men agreed, the captain, the political officer and the brigade chief of staff, but no document confirms it. The Northern Fleet’s mission report does not mention any rules for using the nuclear torpedo, and Arkhipov’s own 1997 presentation quotes only the conditions for conventional weapons in paragraph 8 of the combat instructions and says nothing of the conditions for the nuclear torpedo.

The testimony that can be checked runs three ways. Orlov wrote that Captain Savitsky decided to surface after consulting Arkhipov and Maslennikov. Ketov said in a 2012 interview that after surfacing, the captain, startled on the bridge by searchlights and cannon fire, shouted for a crash dive and for torpedo No. 1 to be readied, but could not get below because the narrow ladder was blocked; Arkhipov, who stayed on the bridge and saw that the Americans were signaling, called him back and calmed him down, and the order never reached the torpedo officer. Shumkov, captain of B-130 in the same brigade, recalled that the special weapon’s security officer warned him that it could not be armed without permission from headquarters.

Hence the suggestion that the real safeguard was not agreement among three men but procedural control by the security officer in charge of the nuclear torpedo. The oral instructions Rassokho and Admiral Fokin are said to have given before sailing (“if they hole your hull,” “if they slap your face”) also vary from one account to another and are not confirmed in writing. In Arkhipov’s seat, what matters is not consent or refusal but whether to call the commander back on the bridge and make him read the situation again.

background.q: Why did the Americans not know about the tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba?
a: Besides the warheads for the medium-range missiles, there were tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba. On top of the two regiments of FKR cruise missiles in the memorandum of 24 May, Khrushchev added on 7–8 September an Il-28 detachment (six nuclear bombs) and three battalions of Luna (FROG) rockets (12 special warheads). The withdrawal order of 20 November lists six nuclear bombs, 12 Luna warheads and 80 FKR warheads. The number of nuclear warheads that reached Cuba varies by source: one annotated edition lists 24 R-14 warheads and 44 cruise missile warheads aboard the Aleksandrovsk, while General Garbuz testified to 183, strategic and tactical combined.

Whether the commander on the spot could use tactical nuclear weapons on his own authority is disputed. A draft directive to Pliyev of 8 September contains a passage allowing him, if the enemy landed and contact with Moscow was cut, to use the nuclear weapons of the Luna, Il-28 and FKR units on his own decision; but the draft is handwritten, and Malinovsky never signed it. The combat readiness order of the night of 22 October expressly excluded nuclear means, and cable No. 76639 of 27 October “categorically confirmed” the ban on any nuclear use without orders from Moscow. At the 1992 Havana conference General Gribkov claimed that authority had been delegated, but the majority view is that no delegation valid on paper ever existed.

US intelligence confirmed the R-12 sites, the Il-28 bombers and the Luna launchers from photographs, but did not know whether nuclear warheads lay beside them. When McNamara proposed on 16 October adding nuclear storage sites to the air strike targets, that too rested on guesswork. On 22 November Mikoyan told Castro that “the Americans do not even have information that tactical nuclear weapons are in Cuba.”

The tactical weapons were ordered out on 20 November, the day Khrushchev informed Kennedy that “all nuclear weapons have been taken out of Cuba,” and they left aboard the Atkarsk on 1 December. Until early November Moscow had meant to leave the Luna and FKR warheads in Cuba; Savranskaya reads the change of course as a response to the news that Castro had instructed his UN representative to insist Cuba must keep tactical nuclear weapons. Mikoyan cited a Soviet “law” forbidding the transfer of nuclear weapons to another country; no such law existed. The American participants first learned of the tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba at the 1992 Havana conference.

C01.title: Two blocs
C01.text: In 1962 Europe was split between two military alliances. The United States, Canada and 10 Western European countries founded the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) in 1949; Greece and Turkey joined in 1952, and West Germany in 1955. That same year the Soviet Union and seven Eastern European states formed the Warsaw Pact. NATO rested on the principle that an armed attack on one member was an attack on all.
C01.src: State Department NATO chronology; Office of the Historian, Milestones

C02.title: The nuclear gap
C02.text: The United States led in intercontinental missiles and long-range bombers. In October 1961 Deputy Secretary of Defense Roswell Gilpatric declared in a public speech that even if the Soviets struck first, the United States could hit back with at least as much force as they could deliver. Scholars generally agree that Moscow took the speech as a sign that Washington knew how far behind the Soviet Union was. Medium- and intermediate-range missiles in Cuba offered a shortcut to narrowing that gap.

C03.title: Berlin
C03.text: After the Second World War, Germany and its capital, Berlin, were occupied jointly by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. West Berlin was a Western city deep inside East Germany, linked to West Germany by road, rail and waterway and by three air corridors, each 20 miles (32 kilometers) wide. When the Soviets cut the land and water routes in 1948, the West kept the city supplied by air until the following year. In August 1961 East Germany built a wall between East and West Berlin, and that October U.S. and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie, barely 100 yards apart.
C03.src: FRUS 1945 III d1206; Milestones (Berlin crises, airlift); FRUS XIV d104, d196

C04.title: Cuba and the United States, 1959–62
C04.text: Castro’s revolutionaries took power in January 1959. In 1960 the Cuban government nationalized American-owned companies, and the United States cut its purchases of Cuban sugar and restricted exports to Cuba, then broke off diplomatic relations in January 1961. In April 1961 about 1,400 CIA-trained exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs (Playa Girón to Cubans) and were defeated; almost 1,200 were taken prisoner. In January 1962 the Organization of American States excluded Cuba’s government from the inter-American system, and in February the United States banned almost all trade with Cuba.
C04.src: Law 851(1960); Proclamations 3355, 3447; JFK Library, “The Bay of Pigs”; FRUS XII d144

C04f.title: Cuba's view of the United States
C04f.text: After the revolution of January 1959 the Cuban government nationalized American-owned companies; the United States hit back by cutting sugar purchases and restricting exports, and broke off relations in January 1961. In April 1961 about 1,400 CIA-trained exiles landed at Playa Girón (the Bay of Pigs), and the revolutionary forces defeated them within three days. Sabotage and infiltration continued across the island, and in January 1962 the Organization of American States excluded Cuba’s government from the inter-American system. Havana was convinced that another invasion was coming.
C04f.src: Law 851; JFK Library, “The Bay of Pigs”; FRUS X d278, d304 (Operation Mongoose); FRUS XII d144

C06.title: Operation Anadyr
C06.text: The deployment to Cuba was code-named Anadyr, after a river in the far northeast of Siberia. The troops were not told their destination, and some units were issued skis, felt boots and fleece-lined parkas before they sailed. At sea they were allowed on deck only for a few minutes at night, and sealed orders were opened only when the ship reached set coordinates in the Atlantic. The soldiers went ashore in Cuba in civilian clothes.

C08a.title: The ExComm
C08a.text: From 16 October Kennedy met in secret with a dozen or so advisers, among them the secretaries of state and defense, the attorney general, the director of Central Intelligence and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. On 22 October the group was formally named the Executive Committee of the National Security Council, or ExComm. Much of its discussion was taped on a recording system the President had installed, and most participants did not know it.
C08a.src: FRUS XI d18, d42(NSAM 196); Presidential Recordings(Miller Center)

C08b.title: The Presidium
C08b.text: The Presidium of the Communist Party’s Central Committee was where real power in the Soviet Union lay. Khrushchev chaired it as first secretary of the Central Committee and chairman of the Council of Ministers (premier). No verbatim record was kept; its discussions survive only in brief handwritten notes by Vladimir Malin, head of the Central Committee’s General Department.

C09.title: No direct line
C09.text: There was no direct line between the leaders in Washington and Moscow. A letter was handed to the other country’s embassy, where it was translated, encoded and cabled home; it could take half a day to reach the other leader’s desk.
C09.src: FRUS VI d65, d66, d68 (delivery-time notes)

C10.title: The UN Security Council
C10.text: In 1962 the Security Council had 11 members. Each of its five permanent members (the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and the Republic of China, meaning the government in Taipei) held a veto, so the Council could adopt no resolution that either Washington or Moscow opposed. The Council’s president for October 1962 was the Soviet representative, Valerian Zorin.
C10.src: UN Charter Arts. 23, 27 (text then in force); S/PV.1025

C11.title: Acting secretary-general
C11.text: U Thant, a former schoolteacher, had been Burma’s ambassador to the United Nations from 1957. After Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld was killed in a plane crash in September 1961, Thant became acting secretary-general on 3 November 1961. Because he came from a non-aligned country that belonged to neither bloc, both sides could accept him in the post.

C12.title: Quarantine, not blockade
C12.text: Under international law a blockade presumes a state of war. So the United States called its measure a "quarantine": it stopped only offensive weapons bound for Cuba, and it rested on a resolution of support passed by the Council of the Organization of American States on 23 October. The quarantine line was drawn as an arc 500 miles from Cape Maisí, Cuba’s eastern tip, and the quarantine took effect at 10 a.m. Washington time on 24 October.
C12.src: Milestones(Cuban Missile Crisis); FRUS XI d49; Proclamation 3504; Navy Dept. Library

C13.title: Guantánamo
C13.text: The United States has a naval base at Guantánamo Bay, on Cuba’s southeastern coast. Under a 1903 agreement the United States leased the land with "complete jurisdiction and control," while Cuba kept "ultimate sovereignty." A 1934 treaty kept the lease in force for as long as the United States did not abandon the base. The base sat on Cuban soil yet lay beyond the Cuban government’s reach.

C14.title: Jupiter missiles
C14.text: In December 1957 NATO decided to station intermediate-range ballistic missiles in Europe, and the United States deployed 30 Jupiters in Italy and 15 in Turkey. The Turkish Jupiters became operational in March 1962. The Jupiter was liquid-fueled and stood upright on an open launch pad in the countryside, and it was considered vulnerable to attack. Seen from Moscow, it was a missile aimed at the Soviet homeland from across the border.
C14.src: NATO communiqué, Dec 1957; NSA EBB 821; Norris 2012 [secondary]

C14k.title: Jupiter missiles
C14k.text: In December 1957 NATO decided to station intermediate-range ballistic missiles in Europe, and the United States deployed 30 Jupiters in Italy and 15 in Turkey. The Turkish Jupiters became operational in March 1962. They were liquid-fueled and stood upright on open launch pads, and they were considered vulnerable to attack. In August 1962 the President asked the Defense Department, in National Security Action Memorandum 181, what could be done to get the Jupiters out of Turkey.
C14k.src: NATO communiqué, Dec 1957; NSA EBB 821; FRUS X d386(NSAM 181)

C15w.title: The SS-4 medium-range missile
C15w.text: The missiles in the photographs were Soviet SS-4 medium-range ballistic missiles (Soviet designation R-12). U.S. analysts put their range at about 1,000 nautical miles (about 1,900 kilometers), enough to reach Washington and other cities across the southeastern United States, and they could carry a nuclear warhead. The CIA’s first assessment was that the missile was designed to be set up and fired within six hours.

C15s.title: The R-12 missile
C15s.text: The R-12 is a medium-range ballistic missile with a range of about 2,000 kilometers, carrying a warhead of about one megaton. Cuba received 24 launchers and 42 missiles, six of them for training, and 36 warheads reached the port of Mariel on 4 October. It burns kerosene with nitric acid, and fueling it and fitting the warhead before launch take several hours.

C15f.title: The R-12 missile
C15f.text: The R-12 is a Soviet medium-range ballistic missile with a range of about 2,000 kilometers, carrying a nuclear warhead in the megaton class. Fired from sites in western and central Cuba, it can reach the southeastern United States, Washington included. Only Soviet troops can launch it, and only Moscow can give the order to fire.

C16w.title: SS-5 intermediate-range missile sites
C16w.text: The photo-interpretation report of 18 October showed larger, fixed launch sites under construction. U.S. analysts judged them to be sites for SS-5 intermediate-range ballistic missiles with a range of about 2,200 nautical miles (about 4,000 kilometers), enough to cover almost the entire continental United States. They estimated the sites could not be operational before December, and no missiles had been photographed.

C16s.title: The R-14 missile
C16s.text: The R-14 is an intermediate-range ballistic missile with a range of about 4,500 kilometers, carrying a warhead of about one megaton. The plan called for two regiments in Cuba with 16 launchers and 32 missiles, and 24 warheads sailed for Cuba aboard the Aleksandrovsk. Its launch sites are fixed and take time to build.

C17w.title: Luna (FROG) rockets
C17w.text: The Luna, which U.S. analysts call the FROG, is an unguided battlefield rocket with a range of a few dozen kilometers that can carry either a conventional or a nuclear warhead. U.S. analysts first identified a launcher in Cuba on low-level photographs taken on 25 October. They found no evidence, however, that nuclear warheads were on the island.

C17s.title: The Luna rocket
C17s.text: The Luna is an unguided battlefield rocket with a range of about 30 to 40 kilometers, carrying either a conventional or a nuclear warhead. Cuba received three battalions with six launchers, along with 12 nuclear warheads and 24 conventional rockets. The nuclear warhead is reported to yield about two kilotons, roughly a tenth of the Hiroshima bomb. Its job is to stop an enemy landing on the beaches.

C18.title: The FKR cruise missile
C18.text: The FKR-1 is a ground-launched cruise missile built like a pilotless jet aircraft. Two regiments with 16 launchers were sent to Cuba, and 80 nuclear warheads were allotted to them. Its range is given as about 90 to 180 kilometers depending on the source, and its warhead is reported to yield 14 kilotons, comparable to the Hiroshima bomb.

C19w.title: The IL-28 bomber
C19w.text: The IL-28, a Soviet jet light bomber, first flew in 1948. Its combat radius was enough to reach southern Florida, and it could carry nuclear bombs. In the proclamation of 23 October the United States put bomber aircraft, together with surface-to-surface missiles, at the head of the list of weapons barred from Cuba.

C19s.title: The IL-28 bomber
C19s.text: The IL-28, a Soviet jet light bomber, first flew in 1948. Cuba received 42 of them in crates, and six nuclear bombs were assigned to a squadron of six. Its combat radius is enough to reach southern Florida.
C19s.src: NSA EBB 449 Doc 7; FRUS XI d171; Norris 2012 [secondary]

C20.title: S-75 surface-to-air missiles
C20.text: The S-75 (U.S. designation SA-2) is a Soviet surface-to-air missile. On 1 May 1960 one brought down an American U-2 flying about 21 kilometers (70,500 feet) above the Soviet Union. By early October 1962 U.S. analysts had counted 15 sites for the missile in Cuba, and they were the greatest threat to American reconnaissance aircraft.
C20.src: CIA official history of the U-2 (declassified 2013); FRUS XI d1

C21.title: The U-2 spy plane
C21.text: The U-2 is an American high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft that flies at about 70,000 feet (about 21 kilometers) to take photographs. Its cameras can pick out objects less than a meter across even from such heights. The world learned of it in May 1960, when a U-2 flown by Francis Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union.
C21.src: CIA official history of the U-2 (declassified 2013); National Air and Space Museum collection note

C22.title: Low-level reconnaissance
C22.text: From 23 October, U.S. Navy RF-8A Crusader reconnaissance jets flew twice a day from Key West, Florida, to Cuba, sweeping over the missile sites at very low altitude to photograph them. Their pictures were far more detailed than those taken from high altitude, but flying that low left the aircraft exposed to anti-aircraft fire.
C22.src: NARA JFK artifact note (VFP-62); FRUS XI d94

C23.title: Photo interpretation
C23.text: Film from the U-2 went to the National Photographic Interpretation Center in Washington. Analysts compared long tents and objects about 65 feet long on Cuban farmland with photographs of missiles taken in Moscow and with material from the Soviet informant Oleg Penkovsky, and concluded they were missiles. That was on the evening of 15 October.
C23.src: CIA official history of the U-2 (declassified 2013); Brugioni recollection (PBS NOVA)

C24.title: The power of nuclear weapons
C24.text: A kiloton is the explosive force of 1,000 tons of TNT, and a megaton that of a million tons. The atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima in 1945 is estimated at about 15 to 20 kilotons, and more than 100,000 people are believed to have died there by the end of that year. A single one-megaton warhead is about 50 to 70 times as powerful as the Hiroshima bomb.
C24.src: Glasstone & Dolan; LA-8819; OSTI Manhattan Project history

C25.title: Warning time
C25.text: An intercontinental missile launched from the Soviet Union would take 30 to 45 minutes to reach the United States, and radars in Greenland and Alaska could give at least 15 minutes’ warning. But those radars faced north; no missile-warning radar looked south toward Cuba. A missile fired from Cuba would reach cities in the southern and eastern United States in far less time.
C25.src: ADC Historical Study No. 32(BMEWS); CONAD Historical Reference Paper No. 8

C26.title: DEFCON and airborne alert
C26.text: DEFCON is the U.S. military’s scale of readiness, running from 5, normal peacetime readiness, to 1, maximum readiness. On 22 October U.S. forces worldwide were ordered to DEFCON 3, and the Strategic Air Command began an airborne alert, keeping part of its nuclear-armed B-52 force in the air around the clock in relays.

C27.title: Polaris
C27.text: Polaris is an American submarine-launched ballistic missile, carried 16 to a boat. Because a submarine moving under the sea is hard to find, it was judged likely to survive even a surprise attack.

C28w.title: Diesel submarines
C28w.text: A conventional diesel-electric submarine runs on diesel engines on the surface and on batteries underwater, so if it is hunted long enough it must eventually come up to recharge.
C28w.src: Navy Dept. Library(The Naval Quarantine of Cuba); Northern Fleet report (NSA EBB 399)

C28s.title: The Project 641 submarine
C28s.text: B-59 is a Project 641 diesel-electric submarine, known to NATO as the Foxtrot. It runs on diesel engines on the surface and on batteries underwater, so after a long dive it must come up near the surface to recharge. It carries 22 torpedoes, one of them a special torpedo with a nuclear warhead.
C28s.src: Northern Fleet report (NSA EBB 399); Dubivko memoir (NSA EBB 75)

C28h.title: A submarine in the tropics
C28h.text: The Project 641 submarine was not built for tropical seas. It had no air conditioning, and with the sea at about 30 degrees Celsius, some compartments reached 50 to 60 degrees; men on watch often fainted. Water was rationed at 250 grams per person per day.
C28h.src: Northern Fleet report (NSA EBB 399); Dubivko memoir (NSA EBB 75)

C29.title: Submarine communications
C29.text: A submerged submarine cannot always pick up radio messages from Moscow. It had to rise to a depth where it could raise an antenna at scheduled times, and because of jamming, orders from naval headquarters sometimes arrived hours or even a full day late. A submarine under pursuit could miss its communication sessions.
C29.src: Northern Fleet report (NSA EBB 399); Dubivko memoir (NSA EBB 75)

C30w.title: Anti-submarine operations
C30w.text: The U.S. Navy hunted submarines with anti-submarine carrier groups, patrol aircraft and an undersea listening network. On 24 October the Navy set a procedure for calling submarines to the surface: four or five harmless explosive sound signals meant a submarine should come up on an easterly course. The State Department notified other governments, including the Soviet Union.
C30w.src: Navy Dept. Library; Navy Department message, 24 Oct 1962 (NSA EBB 399)

C30s.title: Explosions overhead
C30s.text: American patrol aircraft dropped sonar buoys and set off small charges, using the echoes to locate submarines. Inside a submarine there was no way to tell those blasts from a depth-charge attack.
C30s.src: Northern Fleet report (NSA EBB 399); NSA EBB 399 introduction

C31.title: Britain's place
C31.text: Britain spoke of a special relationship with the United States, yet on this decision it was informed rather than consulted in advance. Britain was home to 60 Thor missiles with a range of about 1,740 miles, manned by the Royal Air Force while U.S. personnel kept custody of the warheads. Since Britain itself lay within range of Soviet missiles, it could not stand outside the Cuban crisis.
C31.src: FRUS XI d37; Kirtland AFB note (Thor); Norris 2012 [secondary]

C32.title: The midterm elections
C32.text: The U.S. midterm elections were set for 6 November 1962. Since 31 August Senator Kenneth Keating, a New York Republican, had been claiming that Soviet troops were arriving in Cuba, and on 10 October he declared in a speech that construction had begun on launch sites for intermediate-range missiles there. On 4 September the President had publicly warned that if offensive weapons were brought into Cuba, "the gravest issues would arise."
C32.src: Congressional Record vol. 108 (Keating, 10 Oct); FRUS X d411 (statement of 4 Sept)

C15m.title: The SS-4 medium-range missile
C15m.text: The missiles in the photographs were Soviet SS-4 medium-range ballistic missiles (Soviet designation R-12). U.S. analysts put their range at about 1,000 nautical miles (about 1,900 kilometers), enough to reach Washington and other cities across the southeastern United States, and they could carry a nuclear warhead. They used liquid fuel that could be stored at normal temperatures, and U.S. analysts judged they could be fired less than a day after a decision to launch.
C15m.src: FRUS XI d21; FRUS X–XII Supplement d336, d344

C15u.title: The SS-4 medium-range missile
C15u.text: The missiles in the photographs were Soviet SS-4 medium-range ballistic missiles (Soviet designation R-12). U.S. analysts put their range at about 1,000 nautical miles (about 1,900 kilometers), enough to reach Washington and other cities across the southeastern United States, and they could carry a nuclear warhead.

C20s.title: S-75 surface-to-air missiles
C20s.text: The S-75 (U.S. designation SA-2) is a Soviet surface-to-air missile. On 1 May 1960 one brought down an American U-2 flying about 21 kilometers (70,500 feet) above the Soviet Union. Sites for the missile had been set up across Cuba, and they were the greatest threat to American reconnaissance aircraft.
C20s.src: CIA official history of the U-2 (declassified 2013)

C12n.title: Quarantine, not blockade
C12n.text: Under international law a blockade presumes a state of war. So the United States called its measure a "quarantine": it stopped only offensive weapons bound for Cuba, and it rested on a resolution of support passed by the Council of the Organization of American States on 23 October. The quarantine line was drawn far out at sea, and the quarantine took effect at 10 a.m. Washington time on 24 October.
C12n.src: Milestones(Cuban Missile Crisis); FRUS XI d49; Proclamation 3504

C21f.title: The U-2 spy plane
C21f.text: The U-2 is an American high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft that flies at about 70,000 feet (about 21 kilometers) to take photographs. The world learned of it in May 1960, when a U-2 flown by Francis Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union.
C21f.src: CIA official history of the U-2 (declassified 2013)
